extracted.intended_audience: innovators, businesses, policymakers, IP offices, researchers and other IP data users
extracted.subtask_description: A global WIPO statistical framework and definitions for measuring and reporting patent activity (applications, grants, families, specialization, per-capita/GDP adjustments, office-level breakdowns and technology classifications). Intended to guide interpretation and comparability of patent indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is a set of exclusive rights granted by law to applicants for inventions that are new, non-obvious and commercially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years). In return, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public in a manner that enables others skilled in the art to replicate the invention. This definition implies the three standard patentability criteria: novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness) and industrial applicability (commercial applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications data scope (invention patents only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications data refer to invention patents and do not include utility model (UM) applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility model applications data are reported separately (see figures A53–57). Note: in the United States, invention patents are referred to as “utility patents,” which should not be confused with utility models. Users must be careful when comparing datasets that may include or exclude UMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs non-resident application classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident application: filed with the IP office of the jurisdiction in which the first named applicant is resident. Non-resident application: filed with an office in which the first named applicant is not domiciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions underpin office-level statistics and are used to separate domestic from foreign filing activity. Non-resident applications are also sometimes called foreign applications. Interpretation of office workloads and internationalization rely on this classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin data (resident/abroad) and counting method
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin of an application means the country/territory of residence of the first named applicant. Origin data can be calculated using absolute count or equivalent count; this report uses absolute count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute count counts an application filed at a regional office once. Origin data are partial and incomplete because some offices report only aggregate totals without an origin breakdown; hence origin data should be considered a “baseline” figure. Users should note differences between absolute and equivalent counting when making cross-country comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family is a set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention, interlinked by one or more of: priority claim, PCT national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO’s patent family definition includes only families associated with patent applications for inventions and excludes those associated with utility model applications. Patent family indicators aim to capture unique inventions and reduce double counting across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent family (quality indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign-oriented patent family is a patent family that has at least one filing office different from the office of the applicant’s country of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-oriented patent families are usually considered to be of higher quality and value because filing patents in multiple jurisdictions is costly and time-consuming. Such families reduce home bias and improve cross-country comparisons. Note that some foreign-oriented families may include only one filing office (e.g., a direct filing at a foreign office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family size / geographical coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a patent family indicates the number of offices at which a patent is filed and thus reflects its geographical coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High percentage of single-office families (e.g., 85.6% worldwide for families created 2020–2022) can reflect domestic-focused filing behavior (e.g., China). Origins differ markedly: some origins have most families covering two or more offices, while others (notably China) have very high single-office family shares. Family size is used to infer applicants’ geographical filing strategy and intended market coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-to-GDP ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent applications per USD 100 billion of GDP (used to adjust patenting activity for economy size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicator helps compare patenting intensity across economies by adjusting for GDP; high patent-to-GDP ratios typically reflect high R&D intensity. Data limitations (e.g., missing GDP data for some countries) can affect rankings. Interpret changes over time as reflecting relative growth of resident filings versus GDP growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents per capita (resident applications per million population)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent applications per million population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric complements patent-to-GDP and often mirrors its ranking but can differ for smaller/highly innovative countries. Use alongside patent-to-GDP to understand scale-adjusted patenting activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abroad (away) filings as an indicator of patent value
rubrics_metrics.description: Abroad filings (applications filed by applicants at foreign offices) are considered to reflect patents of high value (monetary, strategic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because abroad filings are costly and time-consuming, applicants tend to be selective when filing outside their domestic jurisdiction. Indicators based on abroad filings improve cross-country comparisons by reducing home bias. The US has historically been the leading source of abroad filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office-level application counts and resident/non-resident share
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of patent applications received by each IP office (with breakdowns by resident and non-resident filings) and office shares of world totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rank offices (e.g., CNIPA, USPTO, JPO, KIPO, EPO) and to analyze trends and shifts in global filing distribution. Interpret changes carefully: differences arise from office practices, capacity, and domestic filing behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Year-on-year growth rate of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage change in patent applications (or other indicators) between consecutive years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth rates indicate trend direction and momentum (e.g., 4.9% growth worldwide in 2024). Large year-on-year swings may reflect policy, economic conditions, or reporting differences; interpret in context and alongside longer-term averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Specialization Index (RSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: An index used to measure a country’s specialization in a technology field relative to the world average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive RSI indicates a country has a larger share of patenting in that field than the global average. RSI is computed using IPC-based field assignments and is useful to identify national strengths (e.g., China and US specialization in computer technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology field classification using IPC mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping International Patent Classification (IPC) symbols to technology fields (e.g., computer technology, electrical machinery, measurement, digital communication, medical technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC-to-field mappings (provided in annexes) are used to count and analyze published patent applications by technology. Note that correspondence between IPC symbols and technology fields is not always clear-cut, so mappings aim to capture the vast majority but may miss some patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published application counts and publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: Published patent applications are those disclosed to the public; published application counts (by year) are used to analyze technology shares and trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication date marks when the application becomes prior art. Data completeness lags: latest complete year for published application analyses may be earlier than application-year totals (e.g., 2023 is latest complete year for technology-field analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications vs grants — comparability caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and grants are different metrics: offices carry out formal and substantive examination before granting a patent; procedures and delays vary by office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of examination lags and capacity differences, application counts for a given year should not be directly compared with grants for the same year. When comparing, account for procedural differences and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time lag in patent family indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent family indicators have a time lag (up to three years) because families require subsequent linked filings to be observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent family-based indicators (designed to count unique inventions) are more reliable for reducing double counting but come with delays; interpret family trends with awareness of this lag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-office family share as behavioural indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of patent families filed at a single office (used to describe filing behaviour and domestic focus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High single-office family shares indicate a domestic filing focus (e.g., 96.7% of China-origin families are single-office). Variation across origins can be due to market size, multinational presence, and filing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of regional offices and regional applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional applications/grants (filed with regional offices covering multiple countries) are treated differently in origin counts; filing at a regional office covers multiple countries and affects origin-based totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin data for countries that are members of a regional patent office will be lower compared to other origins because a regional filing covers multiple countries and eliminates multiple separate filings. Users should account for this when comparing origin data across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model definition and data separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility model: a special form of patent right with shorter term and less stringent patentability requirements; known also as petty patents, short-term patents or innovation patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because utility models differ from invention patents, their applications and statistics are reported separately. Users must not conflate utility model counts with invention patent counts when analyzing patenting activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing routes (national, PCT, Madrid, Hague) classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Different filing routes: national (Paris/Direct route), PCT route (international application leading to national phase), Madrid (trademarks), Hague (designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics classify filings by route; PCT national phase entries are integral to patent family linkages. Route choice affects comparability and counting (e.g., PCT filings create family links across offices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance/renewal as validity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance is an act (usually payment of a fee) by the applicant to keep an IP grant/registration valid; renewal refers to regular payment to keep registration in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents, utility models and designs can be maintained for only a limited number of years; trademarks can be renewed indefinitely in many jurisdictions. Maintenance/renewal practices affect statistics on active rights versus historical filings.
